$comment: Every published number this arm can quote about a competing memory system, with the conditions
that decide whether it may be quoted beside another one. The unit of comparability is a five-tuple:
dataset, variant, answer model, judge, harness. Two numbers are ordered only when all five agree.
`kind` says who produced the number, and it is the field a reader is most likely to skip:
self      -- the system's own authors, on their own configuration
third     -- someone else's table, usually compiled by a competitor
harness   -- one pipeline that ran every system, with one answer model and one judge
ours      -- this repository, on its own harness, which makes it comparable to `harness` only
in the sense that both are internally consistent -- not in their scores
A number without a `source` is not evidence and the checker refuses it.
A harness name carries its answer model when one published table mixes several. The APEX-MEM
table prints its own row at Claude 4.5 Sonnet and three baselines at an unstated model; the
Supermemory table prints its own row at GPT-5 and its competitors at GPT-4o. Those are two
conditions each, and naming them one would let a reader sort across the difference.
Mem0 appears under three deployments -- self-hosted open source, the hosted service, and two
releases of each -- and they share a `system` so the spread block computes across them.
The deployment is in the harness name, because it is a condition and not an identity.
The deployment is a separate field rather than part of the harness name: the harness
is whose pipeline ran, and OmniMemEval ran Mem0 the same way it ran the other eight.

entries.note: The window mechanism's dispatch. Its own reference pipeline scored 43.80% on the same roster, which is the only number in this table measured under identical conditions to this one.
The floor this repository is measured against. It is a retrieval-and-read pipeline with no memory arm, not a competitor, and quoting it as one would understate every system in the table.

entries.source: Mem0's published LongMemEval figure, quoted by aiagentmemory.org and by tools/competitor-sut/mem0_driver.py
entries.note: The number this repository's competitor harness exists to test. A third-party reproduction of the same open-source configuration lands at 49.0%, and OmniMemEval lands at 56.0, so the publication and the reproductions disagree by 38 points.

entries.source: contextier.com blog, 6,787 mean context tokens per query
entries.note: A second self-reported figure with a stated token cost, which is the only reason it is listed separately: accuracy without tokens is not a comparison.

entries.source: contextier.com blog, 4,408 median context tokens per query
entries.note: Paired with 71.2 below, which is the same system read by a competitor's table.

entries.source: contextier.com blog, 2,807 mean / 2,854 median context tokens per query
entries.note: Included because it is the only system in this table that publishes accuracy beside its token budget, which is the axis this repository does not yet measure.
The same table carries the A-Mem, Nemori and SimpleSearch rows below, so those three are a `third` reading of one author's harness rather than independent measurements.
NeurIPS 2025, Zettelkasten-style note construction with link generation and memory evolution. Its published strength is LoCoMo, not LongMemEval.
APEX-MEM's strongest listed baseline before its own row.

entries.source: arXiv 2604.14362 Table 4, session-aware retrieval with expanded sessions
entries.note: The baseline that establishes what plain session-level retrieval buys, which is the floor any structured memory has to beat to justify itself.
No memory system at all: the whole haystack in the prompt. It is the one row that says how much of any memory system's score is the reader rather than the retrieval.

entries.source: Supermemory's report, reproduced in Hindsight arXiv 2512.12818 Table 3
entries.note: The per-type breakdown in that table is the only side-by-side split by question type this repository has found, and it is judged by GPT-4o while the table's own rows are judged by GPT-OSS-120B.

entries.source: Hindsight arXiv 2512.12818 Table 3, scores copied from Supermemory's report
entries.note: Same system as the 90.2 above, read by a competitor. The 19-point gap between the two is the cleanest single demonstration in this table that a published score is a property of the harness as much as of the system.
The GPT-4o floor, for the same reason as the Claude row above.

The highest number in the only same-harness table this repository has found. The harness is run by MemOS's own authors, and it publishes its adapters and run configurations, which is what makes it auditable at all.
Third reading of Zep in this table (90.2 self, 71.2 by Supermemory, 79.8 here), spanning 19 points.
The MemGPT lineage. Its LoCoMo score in this harness is 77.12, i.e. the same system reads almost identically on both datasets here.
Its own paper reports higher; the same-harness reading is the one that may be ordered against the rest of this block.
Same system as the 84.6 above. 18.5 points separate the two readings.
The 38.4-point gap against the 94.4 self-report is the single most important row in this table: it is what this repository's own competitor harness is for.

entries.source: third-party reproduction of the open-source configuration, recorded in tools/competitor-sut/mem0_driver.py
entries.note: The second reproduction of the same code, and the reason this repository runs Mem0 itself rather than quoting it: 94.4 self-reported, 56.0 under OmniMemEval, 49.0 here.
The same system reads 77.67 on LongMemEval under this harness, i.e. almost identical across two datasets -- which is not true of every row here.
Fifth on LoCoMo while second on the vendor table; the dataset changes the ranking, which is why section 8 of the analysis asks for a second dataset.
Self-reported 94.7 on LoCoMo; the same-harness reading is 30.9 points lower.

entries.source: Zep reported figure, quoted in aiagentmemory.org and in the OmniMemEval discussion
entries.note: Paired with the same-harness 63.83 below it: 30.9 points separate the publication from the reproduction, on the dataset where the publication is strongest.

entries.source: maximem.ai/evals, "checked 28 Oct 2026", 478/500 at ~7.4K context tokens per question
entries.note: The highest figure in this ledger and a self-reported one. Its own table is the useful part: the same memory layer moves 0.4 points across two answer models while Mastra's moves 10.6 across three, which is the argument that the retrieved context, not the reader, is doing the work -- made by the vendor about itself and therefore worth less than the same claim would be from a third party.

Quoted as a PAIR with 84.23 below. One memory layer, three answer models, nothing else changed: 84.23 (gpt-4o), 93.27 (gemini-3-pro-preview), 94.87 (gpt-5-mini). That 10.64-point span is the largest published measurement of the reader on this benchmark and it is the number to read before attributing any gap to a memory mechanism.

The same system as the row above with the weakest of its three readers. It is the only published configuration in this ledger whose answer model matches the benchmark's own judge tier, which makes it the closest thing to a like-for-like comparison against the oracle figures below.

entries.source: Vectorize, arXiv December 2025; 473/500 at ~43.6K context tokens
entries.note: Reported at 91.4% with Gemini 3 Pro in an earlier revision and graded by its own model (GPT-OSS-120B) rather than by the benchmark's judge. Its context per question is 6x Mem0's, which is the trade this row makes and the 90.4/85.2 rows below do not.

Neither the answer model nor the judge is published, so this number cannot be placed in any group that contains a system which does publish them. It is here because a table that omits every unstated configuration is a table that flatters itself.

entries.source: Zero Labs, arXiv August 2026; 92.2% to 95.6% across eight answer models; setting not stated
entries.note: Highest published LongMemEval figure known to this ledger, and the least quotable: the paper does not state LongMemEval_S or _M, and does not name its judge. It is recorded because "the ceiling moved" is a fact about the field even when the number is unusable, and because its own eight-model spread (3.4 points) is the counter-example to Mastra's 10.6 -- two systems, two very different reader sensitivities, which is a finding about their retrieval, not about their readers.

entries.source: single-author publication; figure quoted by jakecuth.com/work/agent-memory-lab, which grades it "self-reported without independent replication"
entries.note: Included with that caveat as its source. A 95.4 with a middle-tier reader is the strongest single claim against the "reader does the work" reading, and the weakest-supported one at the same time.

entries.source: quoted by jakecuth.com/work/agent-memory-lab, S12.1 bar chart
entries.note: Coincides with this repository's 83.0 exactly, which is worth stating rather than quietly noting: two numbers agreeing to a tenth of a point on a 500-question roster is a coincidence of two decimals, not a finding, and no group here contains both.

entries.source: quoted by jakecuth.com/work/agent-memory-lab, S12.1 bar chart
entries.note: A published figure with a small reader, below every strong system here. It is the row that makes the reader-tier argument testable in the other direction: if the reader is worth ten points, this system's number is a lower bound on what its retrieval would score behind a flagship model.

The same vendor publishes two figures for itself on LoCoMo (92.2 and 96.1). Recorded for the second time in this ledger as its own entry because the disagreement is about the vendor, not about the benchmark.

entries.source: mem0ai/memory-benchmarks repository, April 2026; top-200 retrieval budget; ~6.8K context tokens per question
entries.note: A revision of the 94.4 already in this ledger and a sharper one: the reader and the judge are the same model, the retrieval budget is stated, and the context per question is 6.8K against the history's ~115K. Paired with the OmniMemEval row at 56.0, which is the same system under a harness that is not its own.

entries.source: quoted by jakecuth.com/work/agent-memory-lab as the oracle ceiling; the benchmark's own paper reports 87.0 on the oracle and 92.4 with chain-of-note (sentra.app/articles/longmemeval-benchmark)
entries.note: The most important number in this file after the roster size, and the two sources disagree: 82.4 against 87.0 for the same configuration. Both are recorded. What the pair says is that perfect retrieval behind a gpt-4o reader lands in the low-to-high eighties, so any published figure above ~92 is a claim about the READER or the JUDGE, not about retrieval -- and this repository's 83.0 with a DeepSeek reader sits at that oracle, not twelve points below a memory mechanism.

entries.source: quoted by jakecuth.com/work/agent-memory-lab; the benchmark's own paper reports 60.6 on LongMemEval_S
entries.note: The floor every memory system has to clear before its number means anything. This ledger already holds 60.2 for the same configuration under supermemory's harness and 62.2 under apex-mem's, so the spread across three harnesses for one configuration is 2.1 points -- smaller than any effect this campaign is trying to resolve.

entries.source: mem0.ai/blog/ai-memory-benchmarks-in-2026: "Mem0 scores 92.5% on LoCoMo, 94.4% on LongMemEval, and 64.1% on BEAM-1M"
entries.note: The only BEAM figure this ledger can source, and it is the reason BEAM belongs here: the same system that reports 94.4 on LongMemEval reports 64.1 when conversations reach a million tokens. A benchmark whose histories are ~115K cannot distinguish a memory mechanism from a retrieval budget; BEAM-1M and BEAM-10M can, and ICLR 2026's paper reports LIGHT gaining 3.5 to 12.7 points over the strongest long-context baseline with the gap widening at 10M.
